<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

</document>
response:
# Review: *Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis* (Achterberg et al.)

This is a careful synthesis. The protocol was registered, the analysis keeps per-hour and per-worker outcomes separate, it reports a prediction interval, it codes work type with tested reliability (κ = 0.84), and it acknowledges that its moderators overlap. The Discussion's main conclusions are well judged: the per-hour gain is real but much smaller than headline pilots claim, the "entirely an artifact" view is not supported, and neither is the "sector-general" view.

The reported numbers are internally consistent. Every confidence interval in Table 1, the trim-and-fill estimate, the duration estimate and the prediction interval is symmetric on the log scale around its point estimate, as it should be. The subgroup counts reconcile: 9 + 14, 8 + 15, 12 + 11 and 13 + 7 + 3 each sum to 23.

The problems lie in three claims that go beyond the evidence, and in what the review leaves unreported.

---

## 1. Claims that outrun the evidence

**1a. "Novelty explanations can therefore be set aside."**
This conclusion is the weakest in the paper, and the Abstract repeats it ("Effects show no sign of decay").

- **It compares studies, not time points.** The analysis sets four studies with long follow-up against all the others. A decay test needs the *same* studies measured at early and late follow-up. Those four studies may differ from the rest in design, hours measure or work type.
- **The interval is too wide.** The four-study estimate of +14.0% has a 95% CI of +6.2 to +22.4. That is compatible with a later effect roughly half the size of the early one. "Indistinguishable" here reflects low precision, not evidence that the effect holds.
- **Long follow-up selects for success.** Studies only get extended follow-up if organisations keep the reduced schedule. Those that reverted, like the five Halden reverters, drop out. The long-duration subgroup is therefore biased toward persistent effects.
- **Design is not reported.** If the four long studies are mostly uncontrolled, their +14% should be compared with the uncontrolled +18.7%, not the overall +13.4%. Against that benchmark the comparison looks more like decline.

A defensible statement would be: "Too few long-run studies exist to assess decay. The four available are compatible with persistence but cannot rule out substantial decline."

**1b. The small-study asymmetry is attributed to publication bias without considering the moderators.**
Small studies are probably also the uncontrolled studies, the scheduled-hours studies and the manager-reported studies, and the review shows that each of these features is associated with larger effects. Funnel asymmetry may therefore reflect real differences between kinds of study rather than missing studies.

Egger's test and trim-and-fill are also known to be unreliable when heterogeneity is high (I² = 81%). The review should:
- run Egger's test with the moderators included, or run it within the controlled subgroup;
- present the +9.1% as one sensitivity estimate rather than as evidence that unfavourable pilots go unpublished.

**1c. "Converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%."**
The estimates being described as converging are largely the same studies grouped in different ways:
- the controlled studies (k = 9);
- the actual-hours studies (k = 8), at least 6 of which are controlled (derivation below);
- the record-based studies (k = 12), at least 7 of which are controlled;
- the bias-adjusted estimate, which is probably also correcting for these same features.

That these groupings agree is expected, not independent confirmation. The 8–10% figure itself is reasonable, but the word "converge" overstates the support behind it.

---

## 2. The rebuttal of Varga & Holm is partly overstated

The Discussion says the controlled and actual-hours subgroups "avoid the problems that re-analysis identified." That is only partly true.

**Some controlled studies still use weaker measures.** The review's own counts imply this:
- 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours. Of the 15 scheduled-hours studies, that leaves **3 controlled studies using scheduled hours**.
- 9 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used manager reports. Of the 11 manager-reported studies, that leaves **2 controlled studies using manager-reported output**.

So the controlled subgroup still includes some of the measurement problems Varga & Holm identified.

**Novelty is not addressed.** Varga & Holm's remaining argument was novelty. Controlled designs don't remove a novelty effect specific to the treated group, and the duration analysis can't rule it out (see 1a).

**Attrition is not addressed.** No subgroup accounts for organisations that withdrew, unless the underlying studies used intention-to-treat analysis. The review should say which ones did.

The review's conclusion that per-hour gains are not entirely an artifact still holds: the controlled discretionary estimate of +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) is the best evidence for it. The rebuttal should be worded to match what that evidence actually shows.

---

## 3. A finding underplayed in the Abstract

**Controlled studies show a statistically clear fall in output per worker: −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5).**

The Abstract reports only the pooled per-worker figure of −1.8% (CI includes zero). But the pooled figure is pulled up by uncontrolled, manager-reported studies, which the review itself shows are biased upward. On the best-designed studies, per-worker output falls. For employers this is arguably the most decision-relevant result in the paper, and it belongs in the Abstract.

---

## 4. Methodological gaps

**No formal risk-of-bias assessment or certainty grading.**
There is no RoB 2 or ROBINS-I assessment and no GRADE rating. The moderators stand in for these only partially, and nothing covers attrition, selective outcome reporting, or the misreported withdrawals in Halden.

**How Halden and Varden were entered is unclear.**
- **Halden:** Was the original +23.4% entered, or Varga & Holm's corrected figures? The rule "where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours" doesn't cover hours data published in a later re-analysis.
- **Varden:** The trial has two strata with opposite results, one discretionary and one coverage-bound. Was it entered as one study coded "mixed," or as two? If two, k should be 24, and the two strata are not independent. Either choice affects the work-type estimates.

**The meta-regression is overfitted.**
It has k = 23, three correlated moderators and four or more parameters (work type has three levels). Reporting "58% of variance explained" overstates what this can show. The Limitations acknowledge the general problem, but the Abstract's "explain much of the heterogeneity" should be softened.

**The coverage-bound per-hour gain is described as "real."**
In coverage-bound work, demand arrives regardless of staffing. With fewer staff present, each spends less time idle, so output per hour rises while waits lengthen. The +6.2% probably reflects busier staff rather than more efficient ones. This matters for how employers read the figure. Describe it as observed, not as a real efficiency gain.

**Sick-leave and turnover findings are reported by vote-counting.**
"Fell in all 14 studies" and "fell in all 9" count studies rather than pooling effects. Most of these studies are probably uncontrolled. Sick days counted per scheduled day also fall mechanically when there are fewer scheduled days. The pooled −31% should be split by design and by whether sick leave was measured in days or hours.

**The fatigue correlation is ecological and underpowered.**
r = 0.18 across 11 studies is far from significant, so it can't show that fatigue is unimportant. It mostly shows that a study-level correlation can't answer this question.

**The inclusion rule is asymmetric.**
Self-rated productivity was excluded, but manager-rated output was included, even though both are subjective ratings. Including manager ratings and then testing them as a moderator is defensible, but the review should justify the asymmetry.

---

## 5. Suggested revisions

1. Replace "novelty explanations can therefore be set aside" with a statement that the evidence is insufficient. Drop "no sign of decay" from the Abstract, or qualify it.
2. Report within-study trajectories for any study with more than one follow-up point.
3. Run the small-study tests with moderators included. Present trim-and-fill as a sensitivity analysis.
4. Add the controlled per-worker result (−4.1%) to the Abstract.
5. State how Halden (original or corrected) and Varden (one study or two) were entered.
6. Add a formal risk-of-bias assessment and a GRADE rating.
7. Reword the rebuttal of Varga & Holm: it rules out "entirely artifactual" on selection and measurement grounds, but not on novelty.

---

## Overall

This is the most balanced document in the set. Its central reading is well supported: roughly an 8–10% per-hour gain in better-designed studies, maintained or slightly reduced per-worker output in discretionary work, and clear losses in coverage-bound work. The main corrections are to withdraw the claim that novelty has been ruled out and to report the controlled per-worker decline prominently.

Read alongside the other three documents, the review settles most of the disagreement. Halden's 23% was inflated by its design and measures. Varga & Holm were right about that inflation but wrong to call the whole gain an artifact. Varden's split between discretionary and coverage-bound work holds across the wider literature. The one question still open, durability, is the one this review claims to have settled and has not.
